en: Puggalapaññatti Niddesa 5.
Designation of Fivefold Persons (Pañcakapuggalapaññatti)

In that regard, concerning the person who both initiates an action and feels remorse, yet does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder—
he should be addressed thus:
“Venerable sir, the taints born of exertion are found in you, and the taints born of remorse are increasing.
It would be well if the venerable one, having abandoned the taints born of exertion and dispelled the taints born of remorse, were to develop the mind and wisdom.
In this way, the venerable one will become equal to that fifth person.”
In that regard, the person who commits an offense but does not feel remorse, and who does not understand,
as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder—
such a person should be addressed as follows:
“Venerable sir, the taints born of exertion are present in you, but the taints born of remorse do not increase.
It would be well indeed if the venerable one, having abandoned the taints born of exertion, were to develop the mind and wisdom.
In this way, the venerable one will become equal to that fifth type of person.”
In that regard, the person who does not initiate [an undertaking] and becomes remorseful,
yet does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder—
such a person should be addressed as follows:
“Venerable sir, the taints born of exertion do not exist in you, but the taints born of remorse increase.
It would be well if the Venerable One, having dispelled the taints born of remorse, were to develop the mind and wisdom.
In this way, the Venerable One will become equal to that fifth type of person.”

In this regard, that person who neither initiates [unwholesome conduct] nor feels remorse, yet does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder—
such a person should be addressed thus:
“Venerable sir, the taints born of exertion do not exist in you, and the taints born of remorse do not increase.
It would be well indeed if the venerable one were to develop both the mind and wisdom.
In this way, the venerable one will become equal to that fifth person.”
These four persons, being thus exhorted and thus instructed by this fifth person, gradually reach the destruction of the taints.
And how does a person give and then despise?
Here, a certain person gives to another person robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; then, regarding that [recipient], it occurs to him:
“I give; this person receives”—having given in this way, he treats that person with contempt.
Thus a person treats another with contempt after giving.
And how does a person treat another with contempt through living together?
In this case, a certain person lives together with another person for two or three years; through that cohabitation, he comes to despise him.
In this way, a person despises through cohabitation.
And how does a person become one whose mouth is a vessel?
In this case, a certain person, when the praise or blame of another is being spoken, quickly becomes attached to it.
In this way, a person is "one whose mouth is open" (ādheyyamukha).
And how is a person "fickle" (lola)?
In this case, a certain person has limited faith, limited devotion, limited affection, and limited confidence.
In this way, a person is fickle.
And how is a person dull and deluded?

Here, a certain person does not know wholesome and unwholesome states; he does not know blameworthy and blameless states; he does not know inferior and superior states; he does not know dark and bright states with their counterparts.
Thus, such a person is dull and utterly deluded.
In this regard, who are the five types of persons comparable to warriors?
There are five kinds of warriors.
Here, a certain warrior, upon seeing a cloud of dust alone, falters, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle.
Such a warrior is one who exists here.
This is the first type of warrior found existing in the world.

Furthermore, there is another kind of warrior here who can endure the cloud of dust, yet upon seeing the very tip of the banner, he falters, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle.
Such a warrior also exists here.
This is the second type of warrior found existing in the world.

Furthermore, there is another kind of warrior here who can withstand the cloud of dust and can withstand the top of the banner; yet, upon merely hearing the tumult, he falters, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle.
Such a warrior also exists here.
This is the third type of warrior found existing in the world.

Furthermore, there is another kind of warrior here who withstands the cloud of dust, withstands the top of the banner, and withstands the shouting, yet he is struck down and wounded in the actual clash.
Such a warrior also exists here.
This is the fourth type of warrior found existing in the world.
Furthermore, there is another kind of warrior here who withstands the cloud of dust, withstands the top of the banner, withstands the shouting, and withstands the clash.
Having completely conquered that battle, victorious in battle, he presides over the very front of that battlefield.
There is also one here who is a warrior of such a kind.
This is the fifth warrior existing and found in the world.
These are the five warriors existing and found in the world.
In the same way, there are these five types of persons resembling soldiers found existing among the bhikkhus.
What are the five?

Here, a certain bhikkhu, upon seeing a cloud of dust alone, becomes despondent, falters, does not steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life; having revealed his weakness in the training, he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
What is the "dust-storm" for him?
Here, a bhikkhu hears:
“In such-and-such a village or town, there is a woman or a girl who is beautiful, pleasing to behold, charming, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.”
Having heard this, he desponds, faints, does not steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life; revealing his weakness in training, he renounces the training and returns to the lower life.
This is his "dust-cloud.
Just as that warrior, seeing only a cloud of dust, desponds, faints, does not steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle, even so is this person.
Such a person as this also exists here.
This is the first type of person, comparable to a warrior, who is found existing among the bhikkhus.
Furthermore, there is another bhikkhu here who endures a cloud of dust, yet upon seeing only the tip of the banner, he falters.
He desponds; he does not steady himself; he is unable to maintain the holy life.
Having revealed his weakness in the training, he renounces the training and returns to the lower life.
What is his "summit of the banner"?
In this case, a bhikkhu does not merely hear:

"In such-and-such a village or town, there is a woman or a girl who is handsome, beautiful, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion"; rather, he sees for himself a woman or a girl.
Or [he sees] one who is handsome, beautiful, pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.

Having seen him, he falters, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life; revealing his weakness in the training, he renounces the training and returns to the lower life.
This is his "summit of the banner."
Just as that warrior withstands a cloud of dust, yet upon seeing the very tip of the banner he falters, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle—such is this person.
There is such a person here among some individuals.
This is the second type of person resembling a warrior, existing and found among the monks.
Furthermore, there is here a certain bhikkhu who can endure a cloud of dust and he can endure the top of a banner;
yet, upon hearing the tumult alone, he sinks down, becomes despondent, does not steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life.
Having revealed his weakness in the training, he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
What is the cause for his agitation?
Here, when a monk has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, a woman approaches him and mocks him, flirts with him, laughs at him, and teases him.
Being mocked, flirted with, laughed at, and teased by the woman, he becomes dejected and despondent.
He does not steady himself; he is unable to maintain the holy life. Having revealed his weakness in the training, he renounces the training and returns to the lower life.
This is the signal for him.

Just as that warrior withstands the cloud of dust and withstands the tip of the banner, yet upon hearing the tumultuous shouting, he falters, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle—such is this person.
There is such a person here among some individuals.
This is the third type of person resembling a warrior, existing and found among the monks.
Furthermore, there is a certain bhikkhu here who endures the cloud of dust, endures the top of the banner, and endures the shouting; yet he is struck and wounded in the melee.
What is his [experience] in the melee?
Here, when a bhikkhu has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, a woman approaches him, sits down close by, lies down close by, and covers him over.
Thus, while being sat upon, reclined upon, or overwhelmed by a woman, he engages in sexual intercourse without having renounced the training and without disclosing his weakness.
This is his case regarding the clash.
Just as that warrior endures the cloud of dust, endures the tip of the banner, and endures the shouting, yet is nevertheless slain and wounded in the actual clash—such is this person.
Such is one kind of person found here among the monks.
This is the fourth type of person, comparable to a warrior, who exists and is found among the monks.
Furthermore, there is another kind of monk here who endures the cloud of dust, endures the top of the banner, endures the shouting, and endures the clash of battle.
Having thus completely conquered that battle, the victor of the battle dwells at the very head of that battlefield.
What is his victory in battle?
Here, when a monk has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, a woman approaches him, sits down beside him, lies down next to him, and covers him over.
Thus, when being sat upon, reclined upon, or overwhelmed by women, he disentangles himself, releases himself, and departs wherever he wishes.
He frequents secluded lodgings: the forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Thus, having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from malice, compassionate and sympathetic toward all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells without agitation, with a mind calmed within, and he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells as one who has crossed beyond doubt, free from indecision regarding wholesome states, and he purifies his mind of doubt.
Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—he, quite secluded from sensual pleasures...
Secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion;
with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters the second jhāna …pe…
He enters and dwells in the third jhāna... [and] the fourth jhāna.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
Thus one understands as it really is: “This is suffering”; one understands as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering”; one understands as it really is:
“This is the cessation of suffering”; one understands as it really is: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”
“He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it really is:
‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’”

For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When it is liberated, there is the knowledge: "It is liberated. One understands:
"Birth is exhausted; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done; there is no more of this state of being."
This is his victory in battle.
Just as that warrior withstands the cloud of dust, withstands the enemy banners, withstands the shouting, and withstands the clash;
having completely conquered that battle, victorious in battle, he remains at the very head of that battlefield.
Such is this person. There is also one here who is like this.
This is the fifth type of person resembling a warrior, existing and found among the bhikkhus.
These five types of persons resembling mercenaries exist among the bhikkhus.
In this regard, who are the five alms-gatherers?
One becomes an alms-gatherer out of dullness and stupidity; one becomes an alms-gatherer out of evil desire and being overcome by craving; one [becomes an alms-gatherer] out of madness...
One becomes an alms-food eater because of the distraction [of other ways of seeking food], one becomes an alms-food eater thinking, "This is praised by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas";
moreover, it is out of dependence on fewness of wishes, dependence on contentment, dependence on effacement,
and dependence on being intent on this very goal that one becomes an alms-food eater.
In this regard, among these five types of alms-food eaters, he who is an alms-food eater relying solely on fewness of desires, on contentment, on effacement,
and on the state of having only this much need, is the foremost, the best, the chief, the supreme, and the most excellent of them.
Just as from a cow comes milk, from milk curd, from curd butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee— and among these, the cream of ghee is declared to be the foremost—
in the same way, of these five types of alms-food gatherers, he who is an alms-food gatherer by relying on fewness of desires, on contentment, on effacement, and on seclusion is the foremost.
The foremost, the best, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent.
These are the five types of alms-food eaters.
In this context, who are the five types of those who do not accept food after the meal has been set aside? …pe…
Five who eat at a single sitting … [and so on] … five rag-robe wearers … [and so on] … five who possess only three robes … [and so on].
Five forest-dwellers … [and so on] … five tree-root dwellers … [and so on] … five open-air dwellers … [and so on].
There are five who dwell in the sitting posture …pe… five who accept whatever seat is offered …pe…. In this regard,
who are the five who dwell in charnel grounds?
One becomes a charnel-ground dweller out of dullness and delusion; one becomes a charnel-ground dweller out of evil desires and being overcome by longing;
one becomes a charnel-ground dweller out of madness and mental derangement; one becomes a charnel-ground dweller thinking, "This is praised by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, it is by relying on fewness of wishes, by relying on contentment, by relying on effacement, and by relying on the essentials of the holy life that one becomes a charnel-ground dweller.
In this regard, that one who is a charnel-ground dweller by relying on fewness of desires, on contentment, on effacement,
and on the necessity for this very thing— this one is the foremost, the best, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent among these five kinds of charnel-ground dwellers.
Just as from a cow comes milk, from milk curd, from curd butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee— and among these, the cream of ghee is declared to be the best; even so,

of these five types of charnel-ground dwellers, he who is a charnel-ground dweller by relying on fewness of desires, on contentment, on effacement, and on this very purpose, is the foremost among them.
Foremost, best, preeminent, supreme, and most excellent.
These are the five types of those who dwell in charnel grounds.
This is the exposition of the pentad.
